name: Ecoauthoritarianism
summary: Ecoauthoritarianism holds that ecological limits, above all population and pollution, cannot be met by voluntary restraint, markets or liberal democracy, so a strong state must coerce individuals for survival. Its writers differ on who rules and how: Hardin wants coercion agreed by the majority, Heilbroner foresees obedience-rallying governments, Shearman and Smith want an eco-elite and Lovelock would put democracy on hold. Later scholars use the term 'authoritarian environmentalism' for top-down, non-participatory environmental policy, often with China as the example.
scope: The thinkers' strand: Garrett Hardin's 'Tragedy of the Commons' (1968) and 'Lifeboat Ethics' (1974), Robert Heilbroner's 'The Human Prospect' (1974, a forecast, not a programme), David Shearman and Joseph Smith's 'The Climate Change Challenge and the Failure of Democracy' (2007, read through Hulme's page-cited review), and James Lovelock's 2010 remark on suspending democracy, with the scholarship defining 'authoritarian environmentalism'. Chinese policy is described only by scholars and not taken as the doctrine. Ophuls's own texts could not be opened, so none of his positions are used. Hardin's lifeboat views on aid and immigration and his views on race and heredity are his alone and are not answered for the strand. Excludes ecofascism.

keyFigures.name: Garrett Hardin
keyFigures.role: Ecologist whose 'Tragedy of the Commons' called for mutual coercion and giving up the freedom to breed.

keyFigures.name: Robert Heilbroner
keyFigures.role: Economist who forecast that survival might require authoritarian, centralised government; the scholarship names him as the theory's foundation.

keyFigures.name: James Lovelock
keyFigures.role: Scientist who said it may be necessary to put democracy on hold for a while to meet climate change.

sources.title: The Tragedy of the Commons
sources.author: Garrett Hardin (Science, 1968)
sources.usedFor: Population limits, abandoning the freedom to breed, mutual coercion mutually agreed upon, taxes and administrative law, private property as the alternative to the commons.

sources.title: Lifeboat Ethics: the Case Against Helping the Poor
sources.author: Garrett Hardin (Psychology Today, 1974)
sources.usedFor: Hardin's own views on aid and immigration (read as his, not the strand's); controls over the commons.

sources.title: The Human Prospect
sources.author: Robert Heilbroner (New York Review of Books, 24 Jan 1974)
sources.usedFor: Forecast that survival may need governments able to rally obedience; limits to growth; population; stationary economy; what a post-industrial order would value.

sources.title: James Lovelock: Humans are too stupid to prevent climate change
sources.author: Leo Hickman, The Guardian, 29 March 2010
sources.usedFor: Lovelock's own words that democracy may have to be put on hold, as in a major war, for climate change.

sources.title: My 2007 'Climate Book of the Year': Shearman and Smith, The Climate Change Challenge and the Failure of Democracy
sources.author: Mike Hulme
sources.usedFor: Page-cited account of Shearman and Smith: liberal democracy an impediment, eco-elite technocratic authoritarian rule, degrowth, reclaiming the commons; their hedging toward a reformed democracy.

sources.title: Coming to Terms with the Authoritarian Alternative: The Implications and Motivations of China's Environmental Policies
sources.author: Mark Beeson, Asia & the Pacific Policy Studies 5(1), 2018
sources.usedFor: Gilley's definition of environmental authoritarianism quoted (authority concentrated in a few agencies run by capable, uncorrupt elites); why democracies are seen as failing.

sources.title: Authoritarian environmentalism 2.0: An incremental transition of environmental governance in China
sources.author: Chen Xiang and Alex Y. Lo, EPC: Politics and Space, 2024
sources.usedFor: Names Heilbroner as the source of the theory's foundations; describes the centralised model and its practice.

sources.title: Authoritarian Environmentalism, Democracy, and Political Legitimacy
sources.author: Yale Review of International Studies
sources.usedFor: Defines the policy model as top-down, non-participatory, government-controlled; liberties eased by mandates.

sources.title: Authoritarian Environmentalism (forum on Li and Shapiro, China Goes Green)
sources.author: Issues in Science and Technology
sources.usedFor: Scholarly debate on the concept; frustration with democratic inaction on climate.
